chapters.title: Chapter 3: Diversification Strategy Across Sector, Stage, and Geography

lessons.title: Sector Diversification: Avoiding Thematic Concentration in Your Bets

body.text: Twenty positions is not twenty independent bets if fifteen of them are fintech startups that all get hit by the same regulatory tightening in the same quarter. Position count only protects you if the positions can actually fail for different reasons.

children.text: Chapter 2 closed with a warning: the binomial math behind portfolio simulation assumes every position's outcome is independent of every other position's, and real startups are not that independent. Sector is usually the first and largest source of that correlation. This lesson builds a practical way to measure and cap sector concentration, without throwing away the real benefit of investing where you actually have expertise.
Why Sector Concentration Breaks the Independence Assumption

Startups in the same sector do not just compete for the same customers, they share the same funding cycle, the same regulatory exposure, and often the same macro narrative that investors either believe or stop believing in, all at once. When that narrative turns, it rarely turns for just one company. India's own startup ecosystem has lived through this more than once.

body.title: Sector-Wide Corrections in the Indian Startup Ecosystem (Illustrative)

events.title: Hyperlocal Delivery Bust
events.description: A wave of hyperlocal grocery and delivery startups raised aggressively, then shut down or consolidated together as unit economics failed to hold across the sector, not just at individual companies.

events.title: Edtech Boom
events.description: Pandemic-driven demand pulled a large share of India's venture funding into edtech, with valuations rising across the sector together.

events.title: Edtech Funding Winter and Fintech Tightening
events.description: As in-person learning resumed, edtech funding and growth slowed sharply across the sector. In the same period, RBI actions on digital lending and prepaid instrument norms affected many fintech lending startups simultaneously.

events.title: D2C Unit Economics Scrutiny
events.description: Direct-to-consumer brands across categories faced tighter investor scrutiny on customer acquisition cost and margins together, as the broader funding winter reduced tolerance for growth-at-any-cost across the sector.

events.title: Quick Commerce Consolidation
events.description: A crowded quick-commerce sector saw several players merge, pivot, or shut down within a short window of each other, as capital availability for the category tightened at the same time across most participants.

body.text: In every one of these cycles, an angel who had spread 15 of their 20 positions across the affected sector would have experienced something close to a simultaneous, correlated write-down, regardless of how carefully each individual company had been diligenced. Position count alone would not have protected that portfolio, because the failures were not independent events.

children.text: The Case for Some Concentration: Expertise Raises Your Hit Rate

None of this argues for spreading capital evenly across every sector you can find. Recall from Chapter 2 that your realistic hit rate is not a fixed constant, it depends on the quality of your diligence, and diligence is sharper inside a domain you actually understand. A former SaaS operator evaluating a SaaS startup can genuinely assess the sales motion, the churn dynamics, and the competitive landscape better than someone reading the pitch deck cold. That edge is real, and giving it up entirely in the name of diversification throws away a genuine advantage.

body.title: Two Ways to Get Sector Exposure Wrong

columns.label: Full Concentration (e.g. 80%+ in One Sector)
points: Diligence edge is real, but a single sector-wide correction can hit most of the portfolio at once
The independence assumption behind every probability calculation in Chapters 1 and 2 effectively breaks down
No amount of position count within that one sector compensates for a shared macro or regulatory shock

columns.label: Zero Focus (Spread Evenly, No Domain Edge)
points: Diligence quality drops across the board without a genuine edge in any single domain
Effectively lowers your real per-position hit rate everywhere, trading correlation risk for weaker underwriting

children.text: Measuring Concentration: A Simple HHI for Your Portfolio

Rather than eyeballing whether a portfolio feels too concentrated, borrow a simple, single number from competition economics: the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, or HHI. It is the sum of the squared share of capital (or positions) in each sector. Because squaring exaggerates large shares far more than small ones, HHI rises fast as concentration in any one sector increases.

body.caption: s(i) = the share of total capital (or positions) allocated to sector i, expressed as a decimal. HHI ranges from close to 0 (capital spread evenly across many sectors) to 1 (100% concentrated in a single sector).
Worked example: a 20-position portfolio across 5 sectors

stats.label: This Portfolio's HHI
stats.context: Sum of the squared shares from the table above

stats.label: Well-Diversified
stats.context: No single sector dominates the portfolio

stats.label: Moderate Concentration
stats.context: One or two sectors carry meaningful weight

stats.label: High Concentration
stats.context: A correlated shock to the top sector would hit a large share of the portfolio

body.text: These HHI bands are adapted from the competition-economics convention used to assess market concentration, not an official or regulatory standard for startup portfolios. Treat them as a directional guide for your own decision-making, not a rule any regulator or platform enforces.

This worked portfolio, at 0.225, sits in the moderate band but close to the high-concentration line, driven almost entirely by fintech's 30% share. Cutting that single sector from 30% to 20% of the portfolio, and redistributing the difference elsewhere, would pull the HHI down meaningfully, since squaring rewards trimming your largest share far more than trimming any smaller one.

body.title: Compute an HHI for a Different Portfolio
body.prompt: An 8-position portfolio splits as: SaaS 3 positions (37.5% of the portfolio), Fintech 2 positions (25%), Consumer 2 positions (25%), Healthtech 1 position (12.5%). What is this portfolio's HHI? Answer as a decimal, e.g. 0.20.
body.explanation: HHI = 0.375² + 0.25² + 0.25² + 0.125² = 0.1406 + 0.0625 + 0.0625 + 0.0156 = 0.2813. That falls in the high-concentration band, driven by SaaS holding well over a third of the entire portfolio.

children.text: A workable rule of thumb: cap any single sector at roughly 30 to 35% of total positions or capital, and aim to be represented across at least 4 to 6 sectors by the time a portfolio reaches its full planned size. Applied to the 19-position, ₹60 lakh initial-cheque plan from Chapter 2, a 30% cap means no more than about 6 positions, or roughly ₹18 lakh, sitting in any one sector, even the one you know best.

body.title: A Fourth Fintech Deal From Your Strongest Network
body.scenario: You spent a decade in fintech before becoming an angel, and it is genuinely your area of strongest diligence. You already hold 3 fintech positions in your 12-position portfolio so far (25% of the portfolio). A former colleague is raising a strong fintech seed round, and you are seriously considering a 4th fintech cheque, which would take fintech to exactly 33% of your current portfolio.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's framework, how would you think through this decision, rather than just following your gut network advantage?
body.modelAnswer: The deal itself may well be a genuinely strong one, your domain expertise is a real edge here, and 33% is still within the 30 to 35% rule-of-thumb cap discussed in this lesson, so this single decision is not automatically wrong. The more useful question is what happens after this cheque: if the portfolio is only at 12 of a planned 19 to 20 positions, is fintech's share likely to keep climbing with future deals from the same strong network, eventually breaching the cap later without a deliberate decision to stop. The practical move is to make this specific cheque while consciously committing to diversify the next several cheques into other sectors, so the strong network advantage in fintech is used without the portfolio drifting into the high-concentration HHI band by the time it is fully built out.

points: Sector concentration undermines the independence assumption behind every probability calculation built in Chapters 1 and 2, since same-sector startups tend to fail or thrive together
India's startup ecosystem has already lived through several sector-wide corrections, hyperlocal delivery, edtech, fintech regulation, D2C economics, and quick commerce among them
Domain expertise genuinely raises diligence quality and hit rate, so some concentration in a sector you understand well is a real advantage, not just a risk to eliminate
HHI (the sum of squared sector shares) gives a single, trackable number for concentration, with roughly 0.15 and 0.25 as useful, non-official bands
A practical rule of thumb caps any single sector at 30 to 35% of the portfolio, applied deliberately as the portfolio is built, not checked only after it is already too concentrated
